For many years, you could put the first letter of either the across answer or the down answer in the rebus square, and the program would mark that as "correct."  I think the guiding principle was that the important point was that the solver understand the theme, not that the solver can mind-read what the editorial team wants for the rebus square.

For many years, people would complain that they didn't know what to put in the rebus square, and I would think to myself, "Put in the first letter of either the across answer or the down answer.  It works 100% of the time."

And then it stopped working.

And now the "read my mind" aspect is a factor.  This is a step in the wrong direction IMO.  Can we go back to "put in the first letter of either the across answer or the down answer in the rebus square"?

Today, Zhou goes two layers deeper.  First, having the letter O represent “Hole”, and second, crossing that O with a word that starts with or follows “hole”.  Brilliant!

What may be hidden in all this cleverness is that Zhou is a superb technician, so cleanly executing a grid with five crossing theme answers – so constricting! – not to mention nixing any o’s in the grid outside of the theme answers.

And, as a coda, she crafts a heart-melting constructor note.

All this has thrown me into a happy-to-be-alive cloud.  Ten puzzles into the Times, Zhou, you have already left a lasting mark.  Thank you for a splendid outing today!

After reading all the comments and seeing so many people up in arms, upset, frustrated, and even angry about the rebus format, all I can say, with compassion and tenderness, is...
"I'm sorry you didn't really figure out the puzzle and missed out on the veritable aha."

It's not just about figuring out where the rebus goes. It's figuring out what the rebus is and how to enter it.

I myself made the mistake of entering O/HOLE per the convention of using a slash when the rebus is a two-way one.
Alas, it was wrong, *because I hadn't yet truly figured out what the puzzle was doing.*

Knowing that rebuses accept also only the first letter, I changed it all to O's.

Then maybe it hits you, like it hit me from out if the blue – omg, the O is the letter *and* the HOLE! This is the moment when the puzzle has truly been solved.

As Barry's link points below out, the only danger from Helium is that 1) it is not oxygen so doesn't provide our muscles with oxygenated hemoglobin, and 2) the method of getting the helium matters, i.e. from a pressurized tank is more dangerous because of the pressure.

From a balloon, with plenty of breaths between hits, is not dangerous at all.  Helium is as far from a poison as there is, but if you don't get enough oxygen, that's a problem.

Sound moves much faster in helium than in air (nitrogen and oxygen, mostly), and makes one's voice high and squeaky, for the brief time the helium is around.  Like David Seville's "Alvin and the Chipmunks".  (But that's not how he did it.)

Grad students often take hits from helium tanks from gas chromatographs and the like.  You just have to be careful, and it causes widespread laughter.

Conversely, sound moves slower through heavy gases, like Xenon and SF6 (sulfur hexafloride), and that makes  voices pitched lower, and Leonard Coheny.

I've never had the guts to do the heavier gases, because they are more likely to cause health problems.  Because they are heavier than air, they aren't expelled from the lungs as fast, so one gets less oxygen for a longer period of time.
